the-center.q: What does Center Study mean by the Center?
the-center.a:
In Center Study the center begins on the originary scene. A group of proto-humans converges on a desired object, rivalry threatens to destroy them, and a gesture of aborted appropriation turns the grasping hand into a pointing one. The object they all refrain from seizing becomes the center: the thing that holds everyone's attention, keeps them apart, and lets them share. So the center is not a mere location. Katz defines it this way: "Whatever can invoke and be referenced by an ostensive sign: the center is both cause and product of the sign" ([The Centrality of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-centrality-of-the-center#p-1)). We are made human by attending to it together, and it exists only because we keep attending.

Katz then distinguishes two aspects. Once a human, starting with the "Big Man," seizes the ritual center and takes over distribution, there is the person or thing sitting at the center and the centrality that outlasts any occupant: "there's the center, and there's centrality, or, as I've called it, the occupied center and the signifying center" ([Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center#p-6)). Much of Katz's politics concerns the gap between the two: whether the king, president or boss actually carries out what the signifying center commands. This is why succession matters so much to him.

The strong claim is that we never get out from under a center. Every utterance, every institution and every conversation has one: "someone takes the initiative, someone sets the tone... and we can say that person, albeit momentarily, occupies the center" ([The Prospects of the Hypothesis](/post/the-prospects-of-the-hypothesis#p-15)). In the same lecture Katz says the first thing the center commands is "to sustain centrality." For that reason he recommends clarifying and repairing our relation to the center rather than seeking liberation from it.

To read next, start with [Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center). It is short, and it moves from attention and pointing, through the occupied center, to the "exemplary victim" and what the center asks of us today.

ostensive-imperative-declarative.q: What does Center Study mean by ostensive / imperative / declarative?
ostensive-imperative-declarative.a:
These are the three elementary speech forms of what Katz calls "originary grammar," taken from Eric Gans's *The Origin of Language*. Each arises from the failure of the one before it, and each keeps a link to the center, the shared object of attention that the first sign set apart. The **ostensive** is the first sign, a pointing that names the object and defers grabbing it: "the primary relation to the center is through the ostensive sign, through which the community confers sacrality on the central object by deferring consumption of that object" ([Programming, Power and Declarative Culture](/post/programming-power-and-declarative-culture#p-1)).

The **imperative** comes from a mistake. "The imperative speech form emerges from the inappropriate ostensive—one interlocutor names the object, but the object isn't there, at which point the other interlocutor supplies the object" ([same, p-1](/post/programming-power-and-declarative-culture#p-1)). That accident can then be repeated on purpose, and it becomes the command. When a command can't be fulfilled, it stretches into a question. The **declarative** answers that question: the object is not here. In doing so it calls on a "reality" beyond the speakers to suspend the demand. A sentence, Katz writes, "tells us, in a highly compressed and largely implicit way, what we would all see, hear, feel, say and do if we were all positioned in the way directed by the sentence" ([Data Mining the Sentence](/post/data-mining-the-sentence#p-5)).

Center Study's distinctive move is to refuse the usual ranking, in which declarative statements are the real business of language and the other two forms are fragments of them. Katz treats that ranking as the error of metaphysics. In his account the higher forms remain rooted in the lower: "the declarative sentence is an inquiry into imperative and the ostensive, the imperative is an inquiry into the ostensive, and the ostensive is an inquiry into the center" ([First Words](/post/first-words#p-24)). So reading any statement means surfacing the commands it relays and the shared things it points us toward. He insists on taking this literally: "there is no way we could ever be doing anything that is not following an imperative within a network of imperatives deriving from an ostensive world and explicated by declaratives" ([Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-book#p-54)).

Read next [First Words](/post/first-words). There Katz runs this grammar through basic verbs such as *think*, *know*, *want*, *do* and *happen*, and shows how much of what we call "will" or "mind" becomes clearer once you ask which imperative a verb is answering.

originary-scene.q: What does Center Study mean by the Originary Scene?
originary-scene.a:
The originary scene is the hypothetical event in which, for Center Study, the human, language and the sacred begin together. A group of hominids, the most imitative of animals, converge on a shared object of desire, most likely food. Because each takes the other as model, the animal pecking order collapses into a rush toward the center. As Katz puts it, such a conflict "can only be resolved in one of two ways: one defeats the other; the two share the desired object" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-2)). Only the second way founds a community.

What resolves the crisis is a gesture of aborted appropriation. Someone hesitates, and the reaching hand becomes a pointing. Others imitate this, and the object is now pointed to rather than grabbed: that is the first sign. Katz stresses that the sign was not issued unanimously. Someone had to go "first," which he calls *firstness*, and this unevenness becomes the seed of all later hierarchy. Because the object seems to hold everyone back, it becomes the first sacred center: "The creation of the human is mediated by the creation of the sacred center as the creator of the human" ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-6)). The shared meal (the *sparagmos*) and the ritual repetition of the gesture follow.

Two features set Center Study's use of the scene apart. First, it is held as a hypothesis, not a proven fact. Its strength lies in how minimally it accounts for language's distinctness: how we can all say "this is the same." Second, Katz insists the scene never closed. Any claim that it ended could only be made from another scene, so "we have never left and will never leave the originary scene, or its worst-case imaginary, which is the very thing which makes deferral possible and must also be deferred" ([Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-12)). Every utterance, institution and act of governance is then read as a further iteration of that first deferral around a center.

Read next: [Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis), Katz's compact retelling of the scene, including how it revises Girard's scapegoat account.

the-sacred.q: What does Center Study mean by the Sacred?
the-sacred.a:
In Center Study the sacred is first of all the center of the originary scene. When the gesture of aborted appropriation holds back a group converging on a shared object, the object becomes something none may simply take and all must attend to. It seems to command the group's restraint. So it is the first being with intentionality: "The sacred being is 'humanized' before the humans are, it is anthropomorphized before there are humans on which to model the non-human" ([Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf#p-17)). This is why Katz calls his project anthropomorphics: humans model themselves on the center they have made.

Katz is also precise about what "sacred" means historically: "a sacred center is one to which the members of the community bring sacrifices." Ritual works by bringing about "the 'miracle' of a successful distribution of the social product" ([The Transdisciplinarity of the Hypothesis](/post/the-transdisciplinarity-of-the-hypothesis#p-15)). Its story runs from animal-gods to the Big Man and sacral kingship, where a human occupies the center, and then to the Axial Age and modernity, which discredit sacrifice and desacralize the center.

What does not decline is the center itself. Following Gans, Katz identifies "significant" and "sacred" on the originary scene: "even with the decline of the sacred, there can never be any decline in 'significance'" ([Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-book#p-155)). For this reason Center Study cannot be straightforwardly secular. Ordinary scenes of talk, science or work are "more in the penumbra of the sacred than outside of it" ([Secular Thinking](/post/secular-thinking#p-15)). Katz even treats the word "sacred" as "a later accretion" ([Mistakenness Revisited](/post/mistakenness-revisited-gablog#p-7)). The more basic term is the center, and "sacred" is one historical name for it.

The practical question that follows is how the occupied center (rulers and institutions) can be shown to be the same as the signifying center, once sacrifice can no longer link them. Succession is Katz's answer.

To read next, try [Secular Thinking](/post/secular-thinking). It asks directly what happens to the sacred once secularism has run its course.

nomos.q: What does Center Study mean by nomos?
nomos.a:
Katz takes the term from Carl Schmitt, who used the Greek word usually translated "law" to mean something more basic: "an originary division of land, a partition, by its first inhabitants." Whether that land was conquered, discovered or shared, "the nomos grounds the community in a more or less equal distribution and a more or less tacit covenant," and becomes "a point of reference for all communal events going forward" ([Sovereignty, Nomos and Parrhesia](/post/sovereignty-nomos-and-parrhesia#p-1)). In Center Study's shorthand, the nomos is the *originary distribution*: who got what, and therefore who has standing, from the center that did the distributing.

What Katz adds is a way of reading every later social fact back to that distribution. "Every last piece of property can be traced back to this," he writes. The work of historians is then to establish "something like chains of custody for the sake of adjudication" ([Nomos/Class Action](/post/nomos-class-action#p-12)). This is why the nomos sits so close to the juridical. A court can settle disputes only because a prior allotment is already taken for granted. "Every juridical ruling involves a modification of the nomos—some property, privilege or access is affected" ([Toward a Curriculum for the New Officer Class Academy](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-19)). In Katz's account, the juridical holds off the vendetta from below and the "antinomic" attack from above, which would put the distribution itself on trial.

The concept also works at small scale. Katz sees a nomos wherever a center distributes. Parents, teachers, bosses and even "the cool kid at the center of the peer group" each "impose a nomos on the scene: the 'fair' or 'just' division of goods, attention, sympathy, protection" ([Identities](/post/identities#p-1)). A nomos is not fixed, either. In the recent essays it can be "enlarged" through new territories, new kinds of assets, and new layers of the technological stack, and much of his politics concerns how that enlargement should happen.

Read next: [Sovereignty, Nomos and Parrhesia](/post/sovereignty-nomos-and-parrhesia). It is short and shows how the nomos relates to sovereignty and to the formal and informal powers that grow up around it.

the-juridical.q: What does Center Study mean by the Juridical?
the-juridical.a:
For Katz, the juridical is one of three basic modes by which human reality is ordered, sitting between the ritual and the disciplinary. Ritual is the oldest: it commemorates the origin and maintains the originary distribution, the *nomos*. The juridical arrives later, with empire, when disputes over that distribution can no longer be settled ritually. Katz defines it as "placing a ceiling on the vendetta by introducing higher order arbitration at those points where the vendetta threatens to undo imperial order" ([If… Then](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack#p-1)). It has two boundaries. Below it is the vendetta, the blood feud of honor culture. Above it is the "antinomic" vendetta, which puts the order itself on trial, "the ultimate endpoint of which is executing the king as a traitor."

This makes the juridical the place where resentment becomes visible and measurable. Courts translate grievances into cases, standing, damages and sentences. So "the juridical is a matter of measuring resentments" ([The Tokenization of Resentment](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment#p-6)). Because the occupant of the center is the final judge, he cannot be tried in the ordinary way. Removing him is a bid to remake the nomos, not a legal act.

Katz insists the juridical is both fragile and indispensable: "no order larger than a small hunter-gatherer community will ever be able to do without the juridical" ([Debt and the Stack](/post/debt-and-the-stack#p-9)). His diagnosis of the present is that it has been "vandalized," turned into a vehicle for the very vendetta it was meant to defer, as in lawfare and the victimary. Much of his political program, from defamation suits to the Thirdness prediction market, is about strengthening it again.

The paradox he keeps returning to is that a perfected juridical order would make crime and dispute so predictable that "the perfection of the juridical would then be its abolition" ([If… Then](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack#p-4)). That is where his later idea of turning judgments into "data exchange" with the center comes in.

To read next: [If… Then: The Idiom of Data Exchange](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack), which gives the definition and works through the abolition paradox.

succession.q: What does Center Study mean by succession?
succession.a:
In Center Study, succession is the central political problem, and in a sense the only one. Ritual exists to make sure a community stays the same community over time. Once a human occupies the center, that continuity depends on handing the center from one occupant to the next. As Katz puts it, "Succession is the most basic political problem: how is the power at the center, held presently by one occupant, to be transferred to another occupant, while the social order remains the same?" ([There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-48)).

His answer is "singularized succession in perpetuity." The current occupant names his successor, and he chooses someone who will in turn choose well: "the occupant of the center selecting not just the next occupant, but the next occupant to select the next occupant, who is to select the next occupant and so on" ([Hyperstitching the Soliciting of the Center](/post/hyperstitching-the-soliciting-of-the-center-and-the-prolonging-of-the-imperative#p-1)). This is also a test of where power actually lies: "To embody power is to select your successor—if you're not selecting your successor, your power is conditioned on the approval of those who will" ([A New Model of Power](/post/a-new-model-of-power#p-13)). Elections, primogeniture and "rule of law" all hand the decision to someone other than the ruler. On Katz's account they disperse the center rather than continuing it.

The concept describes as well as prescribes. Katz holds that anyone with any authority, whether a teacher, a manager or a founder, is already trying to "bias" the future toward people who will carry their work forward. Singularized succession makes that practice explicit. He then extends it across society: education becomes a way of producing candidates, institutions make their own succession public, and succession rituals become the common stuff of culture.

Read next: [Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity). It traces how the idea developed out of Katz's absolutist turn and how it connects to debt, pedagogy and the future. A question to keep in mind while reading it: in an institution you know, who actually chooses the next leader, and what does that tell you about where its center is?

deferral.q: What does Center Study mean by deferral?
deferral.a:
In Center Study, deferral names what happened at the origin of the human. Proto-humans converged on a desired object, and the gesture of grasping turned into a gesture of holding back. That gesture was the first sign, and Katz treats it as the model for every sign since. Representation is the deferral of violence. Katz insists the word is more exact than its synonyms. "Postpone," "suspend" and "prevent" all suggest someone who has stepped outside the situation and decided. But "If you’re deferring, you’re too much in the midst of things to make such a clear-cut distinction" ([Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-2)). Deferral is done from inside the scene, without any guarantee that it will work.

Deferral never solves the problem for good. A successful gesture does not abolish the danger. It only makes it "imminently imminent," and "that imminence of imminence gives us a little space within which to work" ([Lecture 3](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-4)). Elsewhere Katz puts it more bluntly: "“deferral” posits no endpoint. As long as there is humanity there is deferral" ([Deferral, Debt and the Idiom](/post/deferral-debt-and-the-idiom#p-1)). There is "no fantasy here of discovering a formula to eliminate the possibility of violence once and for all" ([The Ends of Man](/post/the-ends-of-man#p-2)).

Deferral also builds things. In the same passage Katz separates it from mere deterrence. Deterrence is a standoff, while deferral involves "allowing for an orderly distribution": the object gets shared instead of fought over. For this reason Katz traces law, credit, property and succession back to deferral. In his later essays he calls credit "the creation of terms under which immediate demands can be deferred," and the juridical "deferring the vendetta" ([Style: Markers and Measurements of Deferral](/post/style-markers-and-measurements-of-deferral#p-5)). Every institution is a stored-up form of the originary gesture, and each one can fail.

Read [Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence) next. It is short, and it works through why the concept has to be this minimal.

debt-and-credit.q: What does Center Study mean by debt and credit?
debt-and-credit.a:
In Center Study, debt is not first an economic fact but the condition of being human at all. On the originary scene the shared center gives itself to the group, which owes its existence and its peace to that center, so the history of debt is "the history of humanity, beginning with our debt to the central being on the originary scene" ([Credit and Succession](/post/credit-and-succession#p-3)). Everything we have, our abilities, reputation and standing, is in effect advanced to us by the center, and we pay it down by sustaining the scene: obeying its imperatives, deferring resentment, transmitting what we have learned. Katz calls this "originary debt," and it can never be fully cleared, only serviced.

Money and credit are later, specific forms of that originary debt. Following Chambers, Katz holds "that all money is credit—any token refers to a creditor and debtor" ([On Credit and the Idiom](/post/on-credit-and-the-idiom#p-6)). Every chain of credit leads back to whoever occupies the center: money is "a 'credit drawn on the sacred,' which is to say a continuation of the originary debt we owe the center" ([There Is No Economy](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-19)). For that reason the work of the occupant of the center, or "pointman", is above all deciding which debts to enforce and which to forgive, and credit is ultimately a bet that succession at the center will hold.

This changes how ordinary social life looks. The "market" view of life, in which everyone is selling, is not wrong, but it is incomplete: to describe our situation fully "you must speak in terms of your debt to the center, what you must pay so that your credit holds" ([Designing Idioms for Data Treatment](/post/designing-idioms-for-data-treatment#p-10)). Reputation, skill and trust are all lines of credit that have to be maintained. Katz's political horizon follows from this. He wants to shift credit away from finance's "outside spread" and toward succession, pedagogy and data exchange, so that debt to the center is acknowledged openly rather than concealed.

To read next: [There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf), the fullest statement of the argument, which traces money from ritual through the central bank to derivatives.

anthropomorphics.q: What does Center Study mean by anthropomorphics?
anthropomorphics.a:
Anthropomorphics is Katz's name for the human science that takes the center as its starting point. The usual charge of "anthropomorphism" assumes we already know what the human is and then project it onto other things. Katz turns that around. On the originary scene, the central object is the richest and most intentional figure present. It draws everyone's desire and then repels their approach. The members of the group get their own agency by modelling themselves on it. In his words: "The human is modeled on the non-human center—this is why I call the human science I am presenting here an 'anthropomorphics.' Humans anthropomorphized themselves before they could carry out this operation on anything else" ([Anthropomorphics: An Originary Grammar of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-book#p-76)). Words like "want," "decide" and "choose" were first used for what happens at the center, and only afterwards for people on the margin.

The term was also chosen to stress that the human is artificial and historical rather than a fixed nature. Anthropomorphics "was also meant to foreground the artificiality of the human, from the beginning—we were always already imitating the center that was itself nothing more than a vectorization of our converging desires turned back at us through a prohibition" ([Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-substack#p-2)). Katz presents this as a deliberate break with the humanism of Gans's Generative Anthropology.

In recent essays Katz separates two terms. "Center study" is the more disciplinary label: it traces how every idiom leads back to the originary hypothesis. Anthropomorphics is the practical side, which enters other discourses and remakes them from within. It "assumes that the originary hypothesis can only find its proof of work and concept in the jarring of an idiom" ([Idiom and the differend](/post/idiom-and-the-differend#p-5)). Katz also describes it as guiding scenic design. The two are meant to turn into each other, like the two sides of a Möbius strip.

To read next, I'd suggest the Substack essay [Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-substack). In it Katz looks back at the term and takes it up again, connecting it to AI and to insurance.

pointman-uninsurable.q: What does Center Study mean by the Pointman / The Uninsurable?
pointman-uninsurable.a:
"Pointman" is Katz's shorthand for whoever occupies the center: the person at the head of a scene, an institution or a polity. He took it from the etymology of "center": "the word for 'point,' which itself derives from the word to 'prick,' i.e., to wound, to cause to bleed. So, I can now replace the clumsy 'occupant of the center' with 'pointman'" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-17)). The word does two jobs. The pointman is "at the point, taking the initiative, gathering all initiatives under his banner, and at the same time the one everyone points to, out of wonder, curiosity or outrage, with the finger of accusation" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-16)). He leads, and he is also the natural target of the scene's resentment. Katz treats him as the latest form of the Big Man who first took over the ritual center. (Elsewhere Katz considers "dictator" as a plainer word for the same role; see [Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-1).)

The idea matters because Katz wants to keep the Axial Age insight that a justice system can itself be unjust, without its reliance on a sacrificed victim. In place of sacrificing the central figure he proposes "the high stakes lawsuit against him, which might be brought by any subject and might end in the ruin of the pointman (or the subject)" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-19)). Anyone who brings that suit has to be prepared to take the office himself. Looking for the pointman is also an active practice. You test candidates and help make their emergence possible, and in doing so you might "turn out to have been the pointman all along."

"The uninsurable" comes from a later essay in which Katz pictures a society in which "we all become insurance companies." In that society the pointmen "might be the uninsurable, because a suit brought against him might so engross the entire system as to swamp any outside spread capable of covering it" ([Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-substack#p-17)). No system of risk-pooling can cover the person at the center, because a claim against him would put the whole order at stake. For that reason, Katz suggests, the uninsurable pointman pioneers "the further anthropomorphisms that insurance companies then insist get standardized," and so becomes "a new model for the human."

Read next: [The Pointman](/post/the-pointman). It sets out the whole argument, from the Axial Age victim to the lawsuit that replaces sacrifice.

resentment-victimary.q: What does Center Study mean by resentment and victimary thinking?
resentment-victimary.a:
In Center Study, resentment starts on the originary scene. The sign that defers the group's rush on the central object also forbids that object to them, so "The first resentment is toward the center on the originary scene, in response to the center barring access to the object itself" ([Accessing the Ostensive within the Declarative](/post/accessing-the-ostensive-within-the-declarative#p-13)). Katz therefore treats every later resentment as aimed, at bottom, at the center. Even when I resent a rival, I am resenting the authority that let him get away with it: "resentment is always directed towards some disregard of the center" ([Nemesis review](/post/nemesis-jouvenelian-liberal-model#p-37)). He also gives a more institutional definition: "Resentment is your fulfilling of an imperative, having the reciprocal imperative you issue go unfulfilled, while not letting that reciprocal imperative lapse" ([Resentment](/post/resentment#p-19)). On that definition, resentment shows up in language and can be argued about. And the response he recommends is to "donate your resentment to the center" ([The Tokenization of Resentment](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment#p-1)). That means converting a grievance into clearer demands for commands and judgments, and away from bringing down whoever holds the center.

Victimary thinking is resentment detached from any such conversion. Katz writes: "Victimary thinking is, most fundamentally, resentment towards civilization—a resentment only possible for the civilized, or those in close proximity to them" ([The Offspring of the Progenitor of Lies](/post/the-offspring-of-the-progenitor-of-lies#p-3)). Following Gans, he traces its authority to the revelation of the Holocaust. Victimary thinking pre-emptively refuses complicity in that kind of crime, but it does so "as a resentment of firstness" ([Deconstructing the Victimary](/post/deconstructing-the-victimary#p-7)). Every form of preeminence, distinction or hierarchy comes to look like a Nazi crime in miniature.

The two concepts are joined by their relation to the center. Healthy resentment asks the center to do its job. Victimary resentment wants a world with no center at all, and in practice it can only call on the state to deploy force against its enemies.

To go further, read [Deconstructing the Victimary](/post/deconstructing-the-victimary). It shows the Holocaust-as-origin argument in detail and Katz's practical answer, which is patient, persistent questioning.

originary-grammar.q: What does Center Study mean by originary grammar?
originary-grammar.a:
Originary grammar is Katz's name for taking the sequence of speech forms that Eric Gans derived in *The Origin of Language* (ostensive, then imperative, then interrogative, then declarative) and turning it into a general account of human order. In Gans the sequence shows how each new form arises when the previous one fails and "linguistic presence" has to be kept up. A naming made when the object isn't there gets answered by someone bringing the object, and that is the imperative. An imperative that can't be fulfilled stretches into a question and then into a statement. Katz treats that derivation "not, as I think Gans does, as a problem that had to be solved... but as a model for human orders that will displace all other accounts" ([Scenic/Linguistic Undecidability](/post/scenic-linguistic-undecidability#p-5)).

The claim is meant literally. In *Anthropomorphics*, which he subtitles "an originary grammar of the center," he writes that "there is no way we could ever be doing anything that is not following an imperative within a network of imperatives deriving from an ostensive world and explicated by declaratives" ([Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-book#p-54)). Statements, institutions and arguments are therefore read as ways of sorting and relaying commands that ultimately come from a center. They are not read as packaged meanings passed from one mind to another.

He is candid that the project is unfinished. The original aim was "to articulate any sign, utterance or sample out of the ostensives, imperatives, interrogatives and declaratives into which it could also be dissolved" ([Media, Technology and Originary Grammar](/post/media-technology-and-originary-grammar#p-1)). Sentence-by-sentence analysis got swamped by context, and from that he concluded that the grammar "could not be complete without grounding it in the center" ([Hypothesizing the Present](/post/hypothesizing-the-present#p-8)). Recently he has started treating it as a technological problem as well, connected to media, imperative exchange and the "stack of scenes."

The best place to start reading is [The Center and the Declarative](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-and-the-declarative), the chapter of *Anthropomorphics* that shows the grammar at work.

big-man.q: What does Center Study mean by the Big Man?
big-man.a:
The Big Man is the figure who first puts a human being at the center. On the originary scene the center was held by a shared object, the thing everyone desired and no one could seize. The Big Man, a term Gans took from the anthropologist Marshall Sahlins, takes that place by out-giving everyone else: "If one leader can throw a big enough potlatch to bankrupt his rivals and turn them all into dependents, then he has occupied the center, not only sacralizing himself but making himself the source of social distribution" ([The Centrality of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-centrality-of-the-center#p-10)). His power comes from deferral and generosity rather than from brute force, and it leaves everyone in a debt they cannot repay.

Katz treats this as one of the two great revolutions in human history. It "unites distribution and political power at the center," and it begins a line that runs through sacral and divine kingship "through the modern day presidents and prime ministers" ([The Transdisciplinarity of the Hypothesis](/post/the-transdisciplinarity-of-the-hypothesis#p-12)). Once a human has occupied the center, Katz argues, it stays humanly occupied. All later political forms are ways of organizing, hiding or contesting that occupation.

The Big Man also changes the shape of resentment. Before him, resentment was aimed at the center for withholding itself. Afterward it is aimed at whoever occupies the center, because his occupancy seems to deny me my own centrality. Katz calls this paradoxical: "the more the Big Man preserves his own centrality, the more I am being denied my own" ([Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf#p-26)). His task is therefore to manage the resentment that raised him up. He has to deter rivals without crushing their useful ambition, judge disputes well and be seen to judge them well, and handle those who dream of restoring the old egalitarian order.

This is where Katz parts ways with Gans. He wants to defend what he calls "the Big Man revolution" rather than regret it, and he says Gans recovered the concept and "then—did nothing with it" ([Downstream of the Imperative](/post/downstream-of-the-imperative#p-9)).

To read next: [Anthropomorphics and Reaction](/post/anthropomorphics-and-reaction). It traces the Big Man from the egalitarian community to the divine emperor and then to the modern problem of unsecure power.

mimesis.q: What does Center Study mean by mimesis?
mimesis.a:
For Center Study, mimesis means imitation taken all the way down. It is not one human trait among others. Katz says it is what makes us human in the first place: "it’s one thing to say humans are mimetic beings, but it’s another to say that mimesis makes the human" ([Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic#p-3)). Everything you know how to do, say or want, you got by imitating someone. So any theory built on a self-made, autonomous individual is, in his view, hiding this fact.

The danger follows directly, and here Katz draws on René Girard. If we learn what to want from our models, we end up wanting what they have, and eventually wanting to take their place. In Katz's words, "imitation leads to rivalry because we learn to desire from our models and must therefore ultimately desire the destruction and our replacement of those models" ([Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic#p-8)). On the originary scene, the hypothetical first scene of humanity, everyone converges on the same desired object. That convergence is the mimetic crisis the first sign has to defer.

Mimesis is also the way out. Following Eric Gans, Katz holds that the sign is itself a different kind of imitation: "the kind of 'counter-imitation' involved in the sign arrests rather than accelerating mimetic rivalry" ([Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic#p-12)). Two people grabbing the same thing collide. Two people repeating the same word do not, because repeating it in a new setting already makes it different. This is why Katz can describe all of culture as an effort to "repeat what everyone else is saying," and why he puts so much weight on pedagogy. Learning is imitation, and he thinks admitting that you imitate is a mark of maturity, not a source of shame.

To go further, read [Lecture 2: Mimetic](/post/mimetic) in full. It is short, and it takes you from Girard's account of rivalry to Gans's account of the sign, ending with Katz's idea of deliberately "intensifying imitation" as the source of anything new.

scenic-design.q: What does Center Study mean by scenic design?
scenic-design.a:
For Center Study, the human is scenic from the start. On the originary scene, a group converging on a desired object defers its grasping, and that gesture creates both the sign and a scene: a center, with participants arranged around it. But scenes do not maintain themselves. Katz puts it this way: "the human is scenic from the start, definitively, constitutively, but scenes, once in existence, need to be maintained and constructed" ([Originary Grammar as Model for Scenic Design Intelligence](/post/originary-grammar-as-model-for-scenic-design-intelligence#p-1)). Scenic design is the name for that ongoing work. The first deliberately designed scenes were rituals, which used bones, altars and prescribed positions to fix the boundary between center and periphery so the event could be repeated.

The concept is deliberately broad. Katz uses it to dissolve the old distinction between "media" and "technology." Speech, writing, buildings, algorithms and machines are all ways of arranging scenes, so he folds them together: "Every practice is designing a scene; or, really, redesigning a scene, or some portion of a scene" ([Scenic Design Practices](/post/scenic-design-practices#p-2)). Technics is therefore not a set of tools we apply to a world outside ourselves. It is "the continual reinscription of the scene—scenic design practices are events within scenes that design scenes in ways that facilitate new events" ([Event Intelligence](/post/event-intelligence#p-14)). This applies to the powerless as much as to the powerful: a teacher designing an assignment and an engineer designing a platform are doing the same kind of thing at different scales.

What gives the idea its force is its purpose. Good scenic design keeps deferring mimetic violence, and it does so by bringing more into view and making what was tacit explicit. It also works against what Katz calls the "Big Scene," the fantasy that all of society is one scene with a single pie to divide. The aim is to translate grievances into practices that others can take up and continue. In the recent essays, that continuity is tied to succession.

Read next: [Scenic Design Practices](/post/scenic-design-practices). It introduces the term, works through classroom assignments as a concrete example, and shows how the idea scales up to tweeting, building and political organization.

sparagmos.q: What does Center Study mean by sparagmos?
sparagmos.a:
The sparagmos is the moment after the first sign has been issued on the originary scene, when the group actually advances on the central object and consumes it. In Gans's account, which Katz recounts in *Anthropomorphics*, this is a release of pent-up tension: "In the sparagmos, the tension generated by the prior restraint is loosened... Resentment at the object itself, for imposing restraint and refusing itself, intensifies the devouring of the body" ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-8)). The danger is that this frenzy restarts the mimetic crisis the sign had just deferred.

Katz's distinctive move is to doubt that the sign would simply be dropped once eating began. He finds it "odd" that the newly discovered sign "would be immediately dropped" and asks "how would they retrieve it afterward?" He proposes instead that the sparagmos was "a clumsier affair, in which the members on the scene try out, practice, and modify their new 'device' as they jostle with each other to get their share" ([The Contingency of the Hypothesis](/post/the-contingency-of-the-hypothesis#p-10)). On this reading the participants do not rage against the center. They "imitate the resentment of the center by using the new sign to block 'excessive' moves toward the center." He puts the same idea elsewhere as "the first trial run of the new sign" ([Hunger Artistry of the Word](/post/hunger-artistry-of-the-word#p-24)).

This matters because it makes the sparagmos the origin of form. The sign is "'flashed' at each point along the way," so that "even at the 'wildest' moment of the sparagmos, a quick gesture would prevent one member of the group from encroaching 'too much' on the portion of another" ([Form and Paradox](/post/form-and-paradox#p-1)). Every later ceremony that marks the move from one activity, or one stage of an activity, to the next descends from this: distribution and the norms that govern it, and later the juridical. The scene also shows Katz's preference for continuity of deference to the center over a hydraulic model of resentment, in which resentment builds up and then discharges.

To read next: [Form and Paradox](/post/form-and-paradox). It moves from the sparagmos to ceremony, scapegoating and the figure who "retards" a converging crowd.

omnicentrism.q: What does Center Study mean by omnicentrism?
omnicentrism.a:
"Omnicentrism" is Eric Gans's term, and Center Study mostly uses it as the position it argues against. For Gans, the Christian revelation unfolding into modern market society means there is no longer a single sacred or social center: every individual becomes one. Katz quotes Gans's own formulation, "what is required is rather the universal proliferation of centers—every human being a center" ([Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf#p-35)). On this view the state hardly needs theorizing. Katz says that this is "why Gans has never had a single useful thing to say about the state," which at most becomes "the field upon which redistributions in accord with a particular balance of resentments takes place" ([Intelligence and Technics](/post/intelligence-and-technics#p-2)).

Katz's objection is that omnicentrism cannot account for its own asymmetries. Someone always goes first, so market omnicentrism is shaped by producers and the people at the head of things. He asks: "If omnicentrism is to accommodate asymmetries between centers, how would that be different than saying that there is a social or final center, with other centers dependent upon that one?" ([Nemesis review](/post/nemesis-jouvenelian-liberal-model#p-29)). A second objection is that no new center emerges out of nothing: "any new center must draw upon the resources and authority of some existing center" ([Linguistic Turn](/post/linguistic-turn-generative-literacy#p-31)). Admitting that dependence brings in a history of centers ranked by precedence, and that is the opposite of omnicentrism.

The disagreement also has a grammatical side. Omnicentrism, Katz writes, "must put the declarative form first," because it has to repudiate some prior command, whereas for his "unicentrism" authority is "first of all ostensive, then imperative, and only finally declarative" ([Linguistic Turn](/post/linguistic-turn-generative-literacy#p-34)). The core of Katz's turn from Gans's liberal GA to Center Study is to put "the center at the center" again: there is always an occupied center, even under liberal democracy, where it changes hands often and attracts resentment.

To read next: [The Linguistic Turn and Generative Literacy](/post/linguistic-turn-generative-literacy). It sets omnicentrism and unicentrism directly against each other and connects the choice between them to metalanguage and authority.

desire.q: What does Center Study mean by desire?
desire.a:
In Center Study, desire is not a private appetite. It is a relation to others and, through them, to a center. Katz starts from mimetic theory: unlike need, "desire implicates us in the other, which for mimetic theory means those we imitate or, more broadly, are bound to through a web of models" ([Demand and the Grammar of Desire](/post/demand-and-the-grammar-of-desire#p-1)). We want what our models want, and so we end up converging with them on the same object.

That convergence takes us back to the originary scene. Desire is the rush toward the central object that breaks down the animal pecking order and brings on the crisis the first sign has to defer. Katz notes that, strictly speaking, desire only exists once the sign has barred appropriation, yet "the overriding of appetite and therefore need precedes the sign and calls it forth" (same essay, [p-1](/post/demand-and-the-grammar-of-desire#p-1)). Desire and the center therefore arise together. Its real object is not the thing in itself but the thing as the scene has made it compelling: "desire is a demand made to the center—ultimately, a demand to be cradled and protected by the center, to have the attributes of the center conferred upon oneself" ([The Sentence as Metric](/post/the-sentence-as-metric#p-16)). Katz also gives a history of desire: "The originary desire is for the center as such—to be recognized by, or even possess, the center—while subsequent desires would be for one's 'proper' allotment from the center" ([Hunger Artistry of the Word](/post/hunger-artistry-of-the-word#p-3)).

Resentment comes with desire. The center that makes the object desirable is the same center that withholds it, and it also sets everyone else on the scene between you and the object. Katz does not think desire has to end in rivalry, though. Some desires are "turned towards the signness of their object, their opening onto infinity," and look for a rule-governed space where the object is enriched by being enjoyed rather than used up ([The Grammar of Desire and Resentment](/post/the-grammar-of-desire-and-resentment#p-8)).

To read next, I'd suggest [Demand and the Grammar of Desire](/post/demand-and-the-grammar-of-desire). It traces desire through the grammar of demand and command, and shows how a demand turns out to be a call for the command that would satisfy and limit it.

attentionality.q: What does Center Study mean by attentionality?
attentionality.a:
Attentionality is Katz's name for what comes before intention: the shared attending out of which any meaning, purpose or self is built. He puts it plainly: "attention must precede intention, and 'intention' individualizes what is 'joint' in attention, making it more of a declarative than an ostensive concept" ([The Worlding Event](/post/the-worlding-event#p-1)). Philosophy and cognitive science usually begin with an individual mind that "intends" an object. Katz begins one step earlier, with several people looking at the same thing and seeing one another look.

The model is the originary scene. Everyone there attends to the central object and to each other attending, and the first sign "is really nothing more than the demonstration of this reciprocal attending to their joint attention" ([The Worlding Event](/post/the-worlding-event#p-1)). Intention grows out of this. As I notice you attending to me, I adjust my movements to fit your attention, so "what is action if not a prolongation of attention?" ([The Worlding Event](/post/the-worlding-event#p-2)). Katz doesn't throw out intentionality. He insists that attentionality is "the prior, constitutive concept" ([Attentionality and Originary Ethics](/post/attentionality-originary-ethics#p-82)).

This has an ethical side. Every scene has what Katz calls the "attentional loop": the moment "in which the participant draws the attention of the others and must put forth his/her version of the sign that will redirect attention back to the center" ([Psychogeography](/post/psychogeography#p-12)). When others' attention lands on you, you can either distract it or pass it back to what everyone shares. Ethics, on this account, is learning to do the second, and immorality is whatever breaks joint attention, whether through distraction or through fixation.

So when Katz asks what is changing in a culture, he asks about attention: "What are the new modes of attentionality; how are we seeing and giving ourselves to be seen … in new ways?" ([Selfy](/post/selfy#p-21)).

Read next: [Attentionality and Originary Ethics: Upclining](/post/attentionality-originary-ethics). It develops distraction, fixation and the attentional loop in full, and connects them to how language changes.

the-sign.q: What does Center Study mean by the Sign?
the-sign.a:
In Center Study the sign is the threshold of the human. It is not a label stuck onto a thing that already exists. It comes into being on the originary scene, at the moment a group of proto-humans converge on a desired object and their imitative rivalry threatens to tear them apart. One member hesitates, the others imitate the hesitation, and a reach for the object becomes a gesture toward it: "It is this aborted gesture of appropriation, designating the object, but no longer directed at appropriating it, that we postulate as the first sign" ([The Origin of Language](/post/the-origin-of-language#p-123)). Put most compactly, the sign is the deferral of violence.

The sign and the center create each other. The sign points everyone at a shared object and holds them back from it, and in doing so it makes that object a center that lasts beyond the meal itself. Katz writes that "the sign creates the center through deferral, and it is a center that could always be decentered—by another center" ([Generative Anthropology as the One Big Discipline](/post/generative-anthropology-one-big-discipline#p-14)). This is why Katz can say that "every word is the Name-of-God": every use of a word repeats, at however many removes, what the first gesture did. It keeps the community gathered around a center instead of colliding over it.

Katz also sets aside the usual philosophical split of the sign into a physical mark and an abstract meaning. For him, meaning is the problem of sameness: "When we speak about the 'meaning' or 'sense' of a word, what we are saying is that it is the same word in its different uses" ([Lecture 5: The Sign](/post/the-sign-pdf#p-10)). That sameness is never guaranteed. It has to be confirmed again on each scene, just as each participant on the originary scene had to check that the others were making the same gesture. This is why Katz eventually proposes speaking of "samples" instead of signs.

To go further, read [Lecture 5: The Sign](/post/the-sign-pdf). It is short, and it moves from Derrida's critique of the sign to the "same sample."

ritual.q: What does Center Study mean by ritual?
ritual.a:
For Center Study, ritual is the community's re-enactment of the originary scene: the moment when a group converging on a shared object of desire defers its grasping and holds the object at the center. Once that has happened, nobody can count on the gesture being rediscovered every time conflict breaks out, so it is repeated in a controlled form. Katz writes that "the first act after the object on the originary scene is consumed is the establishment of ritual," and adds that "we couldn't count on the spontaneous rediscovery of the originary sign every time conflict flares up" ([The Anthropoetics of Power](/post/the-anthropoetics-of-power#p-54)).

The core structure is an exchange between the community at the margin and the center. Ritual is "an exchange with the center: the participant fulfills some command of the center while making a request of the center" ([Languaging Practices](/post/languaging-practices#p-2)). The community returns to the center a portion of what the center has given it, such as part of the kill offered back to the deer-god, and expects continued provision in return. Katz calls this "imperative exchange."

Because the exchange doesn't always deliver what was asked, something has to explain the failures. That explanation is myth. Myth is "a declarative overlay on the imperative structure of ritual," narrating why the center did or did not respond ([The Center and the Declarative](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-and-the-declarative#p-24)). Ritual and myth revise each other over time.

Two further points matter. First, when a human seizes the center (the Big Man, and later kings), that figure is drawn into the rituals. The most consequential rituals then become rituals of succession. Second, Katz holds that sacrificial ritual cannot simply be restored in a post-sacrificial world. What he proposes instead is converting ritual into *practices*: shared activities stripped of their mythical residue, which still aim at results that can be reliably attributed to the act itself.

To read next, [The Imperative Constant](/post/the-imperative-constant) lays out the parallel between ritual and practice and argues that modern history is "the ongoing conversion of rituals into practices."

idiomclining.q: What does Center Study mean by idiomclining?
idiomclining.a:
"Idiomclining" is Katz's name for what Center Study does with language in place of "critical thinking." He builds it from an older coinage of his, "upclining." Linguists describe a "cline" along which words slide gradually from full meaning into grammatical function. Katz wants to reverse that drift: to take worn-down, automatic pieces of language and make them mean again. The verb "cline" also suits his interest in "ever more discernable and discrete thresholds," and "upcline" is a way of resisting "the more passive 'incline' and catastrophic 'decline'" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-16)).

The practice itself is "setting relatively immobilized 'pieces' of language back into motion." Katz admits it always involves error: "You will always be mistaken in doing so, precisely because you'll be violating some convention or expectation, but you also can't go wrong because you present a opportunity for an adjusted response on the part of others" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-17)). The mistake is useful. It makes room for someone else to answer. This connects to the originary scene, where new forms come out of a misfire that others then take up.

The reason it replaces "critical thinking" is Goodhart's law: a measure that becomes a target stops measuring. Katz calls "critical thinking" a "bureaucratized categor[y] designed for mass test taking," and an idiom never does that kind of measuring work, because it is always a naming that depends on people able to "say 'this is the same'" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-4)). So idiomclining means working through other people's idioms, translating them into your own and compressing them, "so as to derive imperatives out of declaratives and ostensives out of imperatives" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-18)). Katz also calls it "the interface between the human and computation." Code is itself a set of idioms, and idiomclining stays a step ahead of what can be automated.

If you want to read further, start with the full essay, [Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining). It works the concept out against information theory, and it explains why an idiom should become more idiomatic and more transferable at the same time.

idiom.q: What does Center Study mean by idiom?
idiom.a:
For Katz an idiom is a singular use of language, one that only means something in its particular and changing uses on a particular scene. He chooses the word deliberately over "theory" or "knowledge": "I have worked with the notion of “idiom” rather than “theory” or “knowledge” because I want to defer the possibility of any metalanguage that is not convertible into the language it describes along with the scenes upon which that form of language is enacted" ([Idiom and the differend](/post/idiom-and-the-differend#p-1)). A theory claims to stand above language and fix its terms. An idiom admits that it is one more way of talking, made on some scene and answerable to it. In his words, "There is nothing in language but idioms, so the originary hypothesis is the idiomaticity of idioms" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-7)).

The concept goes back to the origin. On the originary scene, Katz writes, we witness "the creation of an idiom, one which everyone on the scene had to learn on the spot" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-9)). Every later idiom repeats that event in some form. It is a shared way of pointing at the same thing that holds off a rush toward the center. So an idiom is always organized around a center: "An idiom implies organization around a center such that there are ever new things to point to at the center and that pointing at those things increases interest in the center" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-8)). This is why an idiom can seem opaque to outsiders. The better an idiom is, though, the more it can be translated, by drawing outer circles in and making them carriers of it.

From this follows Center Study's way of working. It does not try to reduce other discourses to a master vocabulary. It enters them, works with their own words, and pushes them toward greater explicitness about the center they already serve. Katz calls this sense of language learning, and of working inside a field of idioms, "idiomclining." In the recent essays he also treats well-made idioms as something like currency: compressed phrases that carry their scene with them and can be passed on and used again.

Read next: [Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining). It is the fullest single treatment of the concept, covering how idioms form, how they spread, and why Katz offers "idiomclining" as a replacement for bureaucratic notions like "critical thinking."

katechon.q: What does Center Study mean by katechon?
katechon.a:
Katechon is not a native Center Study term. It is a theological concept that Katz translates into his own idiom. The "restrainer" comes from 2 Thessalonians and was given political weight by Carl Schmitt; that background is from outside the archive. While reading Raphael Gross on Schmitt, Katz noticed that "the Christian concept of the 'Katechon,' or the restrainer of the AntiChrist, was a very near synonym to 'deferral'" ([Tokenizing Deferrality](/post/tokenizing-deferrality#p-1)). Deferral is the founding act of the originary scene: the gesture that holds back the rush to the center.

For Katz, this gives him a way of "translating into anthropological idioms this theological framing which, it seems, Thiel has found no better 'secular' alternative to" ([Tokenizing Deferrality](/post/tokenizing-deferrality#p-2)). He does this without adopting the theology. He takes Peter Thiel's apocalyptic politics, in which the Antichrist "comes offering peace and safety, but delivers only stagnation and tyranny", and rereads it: Thiel "wants to (in originary terms) defer the Anti-Christ" ([Promise, Fraud, the Options on the Imperative, Messiah](/post/promise-fraud-the-options-on-the-imperative-messiah#p-19)). Katz treats the tension this creates with the expected Second Coming as a paradox, not a contradiction, and suggests that "what is revealed is further discretization" ([same essay](/post/promise-fraud-the-options-on-the-imperative-messiah#p-20)). Restraint then turns into the ordinary, ongoing work of layering institutions of deferral, with no final showdown.

He also pairs the katechon with a complementary figure. Citing a sign in a deferring rather than an accusing way preserves "the difference between pointing as singling out the victim for a lynching and pointing as an act of deferral", which he describes as "the paraclete, or advocate, supplementing the katechon" ([Deferral, Debt and the Idiom](/post/deferral-debt-and-the-idiom#p-17)). So the katechon is the holding back, and the advocate is the redirecting of attention away from a victim.

This is a small part of the archive: a handful of passages, not a worked-out doctrine. Read next: [Tokenizing Deferrality](/post/tokenizing-deferrality). It is where the katechon prompts Katz to analyse all language as "modes, degrees and layers of deferral".

scapegoating.q: What does Center Study mean by scapegoating?
scapegoating.a:
In Center Study, scapegoating is "violent centralization": a community's attention converges on one figure, who is made to stand for everything wrong, so that the collective rush toward the center lands on a victim. The idea comes from Girard. Katz keeps Girard's mechanism but moves it. Following Gans, he does not put the scapegoat at the origin of the human. Scapegoating arrives later, once a human, the Big Man, occupies the center and controls distribution: "Once the origin of goods is centralized, in other words, so can be the origin of contagion" ([Originary Grammar and Post-Sacrificial Semiotic Agency](/post/originary-grammar-and-post-sacrificial-semiotic-agency#p-4)).

The distinctive claim is that scapegoating always concerns power, never powerlessness. "it is always those who have or are believed to have 'too much' power who are scapegoated" ([Aspiration](/post/aspiration#p-7)). Even when the target looks marginal, it is credited with some hidden, occult force. Katz puts it more sharply still: "Scapegoating is also always against the center--even when the occupant of the center leads it. The claim implicit in scapegoating is that the center has been usurped by someone 'behind the scenes'" ([Bouvard on Scapegoating and Egalitarian Morality](/post/the-egalitarian-vs-hierarchical-model-of-morality#p-1)). The original scapegoat is the king himself, and attacks on the occupant of the center "prefigure civil war" ([Thirdness and the Same Sentence](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence#p-15)).

This reverses the liberal and Girardian moral conclusion. If scapegoating feeds on a center that is incoherent or insecure, then you resist it by making the center more coherent, not by championing the victim against power. Katz asks us to "unwrite" the exemplary victim: "to acknowledge victims but deny their exemplarity in order to 'read' them as markers of the center's incoherence" ([Toward a Media-Moral Synthesis](/post/toward-a-media-moral-synthesis#p-17)). In practice this means learning to detect accelerating convergent attention early, and matching power with responsibility so that no power stays hidden.

To read next, try [Toward a Media-Moral Synthesis](/post/toward-a-media-moral-synthesis). It traces how literacy produced the figure of the exemplary victim and what it would mean to unwrite it.

power.q: What does Center Study mean by power?
power.a:
For Center Study, power is not first of all force, wealth or a legal title. It is a position in a scene. Katz puts it most compactly: "power comes from the center, and the center comes from deferral. Insofar as someone occupies the center of a scene, that person wields power" ([Signifying Center, Occupied Center](/post/anthropomorphics-signifying-center-occupied-center#p-4)). The model is the originary scene, where a group defers its rush toward a desired object and a shared center appears. Whoever later stands at a center, drawing and directing others' attention, holds power. That person might be a king, a team leader, or someone who briefly holds the floor in a conversation.

This is why power is unequal from the start. Katz writes: "Power is always differential because some members of any group, in any situation, will exhibit greater powers of deferral: they will be able to stop and examine a situation while others are rushing in" ([Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf#p-46)). The one who hesitates first and models a better response becomes the person others look to. So leadership, on this account, is earned through restraint rather than seized through strength. Within its own scene, Katz holds, such power is total: "Power is centrality, and power is absolute" ([Centering](/post/centering#p-5)). Even the torture victim has absolute power over whether the torturer's demand is satisfied.

Two consequences follow. First, liberal suspicion of power gets the matter backwards. Power is not something to be checked from outside; someone always occupies the center, and the real question is whether they occupy it well. Second, the governing test becomes matching power with responsibility: "if you give someone the responsibility to carry out some task or function, you must give them the power they need to do it" ([Disciplining Disciplines](/post/disciplining-disciplines#p-13)). In later essays this widens into succession, meaning that the surest sign power is truly held is that its holder names a successor.

To read next, [Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf) is the fullest treatment. It traces power from the originary scene through rights, resentment and succession.

sovereignty.q: What does Center Study mean by sovereignty?
sovereignty.a:
For Center Study, sovereignty is the political form taken by the center once a human being occupies it. On the originary scene there is no sovereign, only a shared center that halts the rush toward violence. When the Big Man seizes that center and takes over distribution, the question of who decides becomes unavoidable. Katz pares the concept down deliberately: "the model of sovereignty is, simply, sovereignty: someone who decides what it means to say friend or enemy, law abiding or criminal, loyal or treasonous, permitted or forbidden, and everyone knows who this someone is, what he decides, and that he can do what he decides" ([The Originary Hypothesis and Reactionary Thinking](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-and-reactionary-thinking#p-17)). Sovereignty in this sense keeps alive the moment on the originary scene when deferral won out.

The anthropological ground is that "the center is never absent" ([The Anthropoetics of Power](/post/the-anthropoetics-of-power#p-63)). Sovereignty is conserved: any reform you can imagine assumes someone at the center who would carry it out or allow it. For Katz, appeals to "the people," rights or the constitution do not do away with sovereignty. He calls them "super-sovereignties," and what they actually do is divide it, so that factions compete to fill what he calls a "phantom sovereign."

His most distinctive move is to make sovereignty a matter of time. The surest sign that power is really held is that "the sovereign selected his successor" ([Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-1)). The aim is singularized succession in perpetuity: an occupant who chooses a successor able to choose a successor, and so on. This reshapes the old objection that sovereigns can't command just anything. Katz's answer is that what resists a sovereign's command is mostly "prior acts of sovereignty" ([The Temporality of Sovereignty](/post/the-temporality-of-sovereignty#p-6)), that is, decisions inherited from earlier occupants, not some spontaneous social order outside the center.

In the recent essays, sovereignty is folded into a broader project that ties together succession, finance and technology. There Katz suggests that whoever secures and curates data most reliably comes to occupy the center.

Read next: [The Temporality of Sovereignty](/post/the-temporality-of-sovereignty). It is short, takes on the strongest objection directly, and sets out how a whole social order might be organized around succession.

money.q: What does Center Study mean by money?
money.a:
For Center Study, money is not a neutral medium that grew out of barter between self-interested traders. It is a form taken by our debt to the center. In the essay Katz wrote with Zack Baker, "Money records, by the center, a debt paid to the center, and that record can in turn become a way of paying debts to the center" ([There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-36)). Money begins as a token of what each contributes to a shared order: provisions for a sacrifice, men and supplies for a war. Only afterwards does it circulate among the people at the margins.

Money is therefore always a matter of power. In *Anthropomorphics* Katz calls it "a form taken by the delegation of power, and is therefore a form of power itself" ([The Generativity of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-generativity-of-the-center#p-18)). The ruler sets up markets and issues coin so that activity he does not supervise directly still refers back to him. A sum of money stands for access to a piece of the center. Its value depends on the center lasting: "Orderly succession lies in the background of money—if anyone could seize power at any time then it would be impossible to rely on money—it wouldn’t work" ([Learncoin](/post/learncoin#p-1)).

This gives Katz a historical diagnosis. The modern, capitalist form of money began in late seventeenth-century England, when the Bank of England became the government's creditor. From that point the occupant of the center depends on the "outside spread" of finance, and economics presents self-interest as the origin of the social order. Katz takes this as a reason to think about what could replace money. His candidates are data exchange and "learncoin", meaning credit tied to teaching, apprenticeship and succession rather than to expected future earnings.

To read next: [There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf), which works through money, banking, derivatives and succession in one sustained argument.

media.q: What does Center Study mean by media?
media.a:
For Center Study, a medium is whatever holds a scene together so that a sign can mean something on it. Katz sets this against McLuhan's "extension of man," which still assumes a man there to be extended. His counter-claim is "that media is scenic design" ([On the Existence of World Scenes](/post/on-the-existence-of-world-scenes#p-2)). The first medium is the originary scene itself: "a set of invisible lines we could hypothetically draw connecting the sensorium of each of the scene's participants to each other's" ([Mediated Centrality](/post/anthropomorphics-mediated-centrality#p-11)). Every later medium tries to rebuild those lines across distance and time.

This gives a simple account of media history. Each new medium makes up for what was lost in moving from the previous one. When speech is written down, the speaker's tone disappears, so writing adds words like "cautiously" or "insistently" to restore it: "Whatever is lost in the previous medium one tries to replace in the new medium" ([The Declarative Order and Inquiry](/post/the-declarative-order-and-inquiry#p-11)). Literacy, print, film and screens are then layers of supplement, each holding readers or viewers on a shared scene, more or less convincingly.

Media are therefore never neutral channels. They are bound up with the center and with power: "Technology is governance, and so is media" ([Programming and Visuality](/post/programming-and-visuality-toward-inscipto-punctual-cultivation#p-1)). In recent essays Katz distinguishes media from technology by grammar. Technology tries to shorten the exchange between a command and its fulfilment, while media draws that exchange out, "the more prolonged and inconclusive the imperative exchange... the more we are talking of media" ([Media, Technology and Originary Grammar](/post/media-technology-and-originary-grammar#p-20)). On this view, news and social media are where questions, accusations and judgments about the center multiply.

To read next, start with [Mediated Centrality](/post/anthropomorphics-mediated-centrality). It is the *Anthropomorphics* chapter that builds this theory from the originary scene.

technology.q: What does Center Study mean by technology?
technology.a:
In Center Study, technology is not a neutral set of tools that free individuals pick up and put to use. It is a form of governance, grounded in the imperative, the speech act of commanding and obeying. Katz traces it back past machines to ritual, where everyone on the scene is arranged so that something happens: "the first technology is ritual, in which words—prayers, imprecations, blessings, etc.—make things happen on a scene" ([The Grammar of Technology](/post/the-grammar-of-technology-substack#p-1)). Technology in the full sense starts "as soon as an imperative is extended past the immediate relation between imperator and imperatee" and "puts people to work, makes them 'part' of a 'whole'" (/post/the-grammar-of-technology-substack#p-4). The first large-scale cases were the slave and conscript armies of the ancient empires. Machines came later, modeled on how those masses were coordinated.

That is why Katz's main formula is "the perfection of the imperative": each innovation breaks a command into smaller commands that one piece of machinery passes to another, until a whole sequence runs without anyone stepping in. Two terms go with this. The first is *scenic design*: technology builds and rebuilds the scenes we stand on. The second is the *stack of scenes*: scenes nested inside other scenes, with each layer handing work to the others. As he puts it, "Any governance is to some extent 'technocracy' and any technology is governance" ([Hyperstitching…](/post/hyperstitching-the-soliciting-of-the-center-and-the-prolonging-of-the-imperative#p-7)).

The most hopeful version of the idea is pedagogical. Automating a human activity means studying that activity closely, which turns up new capacities, which can then be taught. So "the real 'meaning' of technology is the erection of 'pedagogical platforms' in which ever more complex modes of deferral are invented and tested" ([Debt and the Stack](/post/debt-and-the-stack#p-11)). Here deferral means holding back the rush toward conflict, the move that Center Study places at the origin of language. Technology is also the way post-sacred orders keep their continuity while the people at the center keep changing ([Intelligence and Technics](/post/intelligence-and-technics#p-7)).

For the clearest single account, read [Originary Technics](/post/originary-technics). It derives technology from the imperative step by step and ties it to succession, the question of who carries a practice forward after you.

event.q: What does Center Study mean by event?
event.a:
For Katz, an event is not just anything that occurs. He gives what he calls a "strong definition": an event is "something that happens and that can’t be reduced to, or wouldn’t have been predictable by, its “parts” or prior events. An event is something new" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-21)). He argues that you can only break an event into parts, or predict it, after the fact. By then it has already been closed off and framed, and that closing and framing is itself part of the event.

The model for every event is the originary one. "The simplest answer is that the human emerged in an event" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-25)). Language could not have accumulated bit by bit. Some threshold had to be crossed, all at once, when the gesture of deferral "took" around a shared object. For this reason Katz ties event and center closely together: "There are events because there are centers, and centers because there are events" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-17)). Something counts as significant and memorable, something that leaves a mark, only because attention has gathered around a center. And every center was founded in some event.

He also pairs event with scene, and the two are easy to confuse. A scene is the existing arrangement of positions, signs and marks. An event is what rearranges it: "the scene is the articulation of inscriptions enabling a new inscription while the event is the new inscription that re-inscribes all the existing ones" ([Event Intelligence](/post/event-intelligence#p-13)). In that same essay Katz notes that GA has talked a great deal about scenes and very little about events, and he sets out to correct this. For practical purposes, an event is a gesture that makes something new visible to everyone on the scene, so that the scene becomes a different one.

To read next: [Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center). It begins with how news "stories" are built and works back to the originary event, so it shows the concept applied to ordinary current affairs.

charisma.q: What does Center Study mean by charisma?
charisma.a:
In Center Study, charisma names the power that gathers around someone who defers more than others can. Katz takes the term from Philip Rieff (an outside source, though one he cites throughout) and fits it into the originary scene: whoever restrains desire, resentment or the rush toward an object becomes a center for everyone else. Rieff's charisma is, in Katz's gloss, "the magnetic effect of a display of deferral and discipline beyond the capacity of the onlooker, in which one oscillates between exploiting the 'leader''s vulnerability and taking him as a model" ([A Kind of Apocalyptic Politics](/post/a-kind-of-apocalyptic-politics#p-4)). Charisma is therefore a source of power, and it is also exposed to attack.

Katz distinguishes two charismas. "Graceful" charisma is "deferral in obedience to an absolute imperative (in our terms, the imperative to defer violent centralizing)" ([Beyond "Post-Sacrificial"](/post/beyond-post-sacrificial#p-12)). We confer it on the center through the way we obey, closing the gap "between the imperative issued and the imperative obeyed" ([Form and Paradox](/post/form-and-paradox#p-5)). The modern, post-Weberian charisma reverses this. It means "the transgression of the established, the secure, and the accepted" ([The Two Charismas](/post/the-two-charismas#p-3)). Transgressive charisma is gained by violently centralizing someone who is accused of falsely claiming centrality, and you can recognise it because "its bearer will accuse his target of all of the violations of normative order that he himself commits in his very accusation" ([Form and Paradox](/post/form-and-paradox#p-6)).

This is why charisma matters to Katz's account of the left. In his reading, those who display restraint and so generate a center "are attacked for having stolen that centrality" ([Toward a Unified Field Theory of the Left](/post/toward-a-unified-field-theory-of-the-left#p-25)). Katz also concedes that the two forms are hard to tell apart in practice, because transgression can present itself as restraint, and the defence of tradition can carry its own transgressive thrill.

To read next, start with [Form and Paradox](/post/form-and-paradox). It sets the two charismas on the originary scene and ends with the figure of the "retardant", the one who hesitates and slows the crowd down. That figure is graceful charisma in practice.

narrative.q: What does Center Study mean by narrative?
narrative.a:
For Center Study, narrative is the continuation of myth. Myth arose to explain why ritual failed: the community gave the center what it asked, and when the center did not deliver, a story had to account for the gap. Narrative inherits this job, and with it a sacrificial structure. Katz is blunt: "Narrative is always sacrificial, regardless of the best efforts of its most sophisticated practitioners" ([Hypothesis/Practice Vs. Narrative](/post/hypothesis-practice-vs-narrative-the-iterative-center-gablog#p-8)). A protagonist, rivals and expendable extras, a conflict leading to a payoff: that shape is the shape of the scene converging on a victim.

Narrative is also, for Katz, how we represent mimetic desire. A story "hooks" us by making us take sides, and taking sides inflames desires and resentments we would not otherwise have. At the scale of politics this becomes the Big Scene: "every narrative follows a protagonist, individual or collective, from having or lacking its piece of the central pie, to losing or gaining more of the pie" ([Stacking Against the Big Scene](/post/stacking-against-the-big-scene#p-13)). The Big Scene imagines the whole of society as a single scene with one pie, and that is why it can only produce resentment.

Katz does not recommend fleeing into "abstract" thinking, which only breaks the big story into many smaller ones. His alternative is the pairing of practice and hypothesis, which stands to narrative as myth stood to ritual. You treat events as overlapping scenes, so that "the beginning of one narrative is the middle of another and the end of yet another—in situating ourselves at that point we exempt ourselves, presently at least, from all of them" ([Narrative](/post/narrative#p-20)). From there you can resist the most malignant story, the one "with the too-convenient bad guy," and enter other people's narratives on your own terms rather than appearing as an extra in theirs.
