Read next: [Narrative](/post/narrative). It is short, works through media "framing" with concrete examples, and shows how to put your opponents inside your narrative instead of being placed inside theirs.

capital.q: What does Center Study mean by capital?
capital.a:
For Center Study, capital is not an "economy" standing beneath politics. It is a mode of power, a way of occupying and steering the center after sacral kingship has broken down. Katz reverses the secular habit of treating markets and property as the base: "Starting with the center, as both occupied and signifying, reverses this approach. Now we can see all these concepts as the results of delegations on the part of central authority" ([Center and Distribution](/post/anthropomorphics-center-and-distribution#p-1)).

What sets capital apart from money is its reach. Money is a claim on a portion of distribution. Capital works on the institutions that produce knowledge and personnel: "if money represents power over a piece of the center, capital represents power over the disciplines" ([Money and Capital as Media and Power](/post/money-and-capital-as-media-and-power#p-8)). It does this by abstraction: "the power to abstract individuals, groups and perhaps most importantly of all, entire disciplines, from the traditions and communities within which they are embedded so as to introduce them into new hierarchies" ([Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-book#p-308)). Katz takes over Bichler and Nitzan's definition: value is expected future earnings discounted to the present. The owner's real power lies in being able to secure the conditions under which those earnings will arrive, which means governments, media and regulation are capitalized along with the land or the firm.

This connects capital to the question at the heart of Center Study, which is succession. "Capital is a distribution of power aimed at solving the succession problem by constraining the possibilities—no ruler can rule against capital" ([Successful Succession](/post/successful-succession#p-14)). Under the central bank, occupants of the center rotate, but only within the limits that preserve opportunities for the strongest capitalizers. Katz's alternative is to tie value to continuity of succession instead. In practice this means converting assets into data and backing value with "pedagogical futures", that is, wagers on how people are trained and recruited to succeed one another, rather than with earnings that are discounted and then cashed out.

Read next: [Money and Capital as Media and Power](/post/money-and-capital-as-media-and-power). It sets money, capital and power side by side as competing media for listening to the center.

firstness.q: What does Center Study mean by firstness?
firstness.a:
Firstness names a simple fact that Katz treats as basic: on any scene, someone has to go first. As he puts it, "in any form of social organization or coordination, someone will go first, simply because everyone can't do the same thing at the same time—this is what "firstness" means" ([Tokenization](/post/tokenization#p-15)). Someone starts the conversation, someone notices the emergency, someone sets the tone, and everyone after them works on a field that this first move has shaped.

The concept goes back to the originary scene itself. Gans first developed it (his essay "On Firstness" is in the volume Katz edited). Katz takes it further. Gans's account can make it sound as though everyone issued the sign together, but Katz argues that "someone on the originary scene had to emit the sign first, albeit in a way that could not be recognized as such until it has circulated among the group" ([The Contingency of the Hypothesis](/post/the-contingency-of-the-hypothesis#p-11)). If all had signed at the same moment, the sign would look like an instinct rather than an event. So asymmetry belongs to the human from its origin. As Katz says elsewhere, firstness "simply points to the sceneness of the scene": things happen first, then second, then third ([The Holy Grammar of Presence](/post/the-holy-grammar-of-presence#p-6)).

This is why firstness matters for Center Study's politics and its account of resentment. Equality, on Katz's reading, never removes firstness; it only hides it. "Egalitarianism is merely fractal hierarchy," he writes, and imagining spontaneous collective action serves "to erase the firstness and minimize the resentments" it provokes ([Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-book#p-83)). Firstness grows into "centered ordinality" (first, second, third, and so on, arranged around a center) and finally into the Big Man and the problem of succession. Victimary thinking, by contrast, reads every instance of firstness as usurpation.

Read [The Contingency of the Hypothesis](/post/the-contingency-of-the-hypothesis) next. It shows why Katz insists on an uneven originary scene, and why that insistence led him away from Gans's version.

market.q: What does Center Study mean by market?
market.a:
For Center Study the market is not a self-generating order of free individuals that the state merely protects. It is a margin of the center. Katz's working definition is that the market is "what people without direct authority for maintaining the social center do with knowledge, information and skills when they are being protected and bounded but not directly supervised by such authorities" ([Market Capillarism](/post/market-capillarism-gablog#p-1)). Markets exist because supervision can never be total. Any command leaves a gap in how it gets carried out, and exchange fills that gap. Historically, too, markets are made from above: "Markets represent forms of delegation by the central authority—markets are areas of social life that are not under direct sovereign supervision" ([The Generativity of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-generativity-of-the-center#p-17)).

This reverses the liberal picture. Katz grants the Hayekian point that no center can know everything, but he draws a modest conclusion from it. The case for markets "is really saying no more than that you can't do a very good job if you're being micromanaged at every point along the way," and "it's equally true that you can't do a very good job if the terms of each move you make have to be 'negotiated' with a constantly changing range of agents" ([Center and Distribution](/post/anthropomorphics-center-and-distribution#p-25)). The central authority can loosen or tighten supervision for its own purposes. One such purpose is to let talented people work as "skunkworks," that is, to see what they can do when they are left alone ([The Event of Technology](/post/the-event-of-technology-gablog#p-14)).

The trouble starts when this relation is forgotten. Liberalism, Katz argues, teaches that what happens below the threshold of supervision determines the supervision itself. Money and capital then become rival powers that bend the center, rather than signs of what the center has delegated. Later essays go further and call "the 'economy'" "nothing more than an ideological representation of our more primary debt relationship with the center" ([There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-2)).

Read next: [Market Capillarism](/post/market-capillarism-gablog). It is a short post that sets out the definition and the two-sided character of every market act, which partly serves the authority of the center and partly tries to bend that authority to its own incentives.

disciplinarity.q: What does Center Study mean by disciplinarity?
disciplinarity.a:
For Katz, disciplinarity is the originary scene seen as a practice we keep repeating. A discipline is any scene of joint attention organized around a center, where people hold off appropriating what they are attending to so that it can show them something. That is why he can say that "discipline is simply a more deliberate form of deferral" ([Learning, Discipline and the Thought Experiment](/post/learning-discipline-and-the-thought-experiment#p-10)). He also pushes the claim back to the origin itself: "there is nothing but disciplinarity: disciplinarity is coextensive with the human: the originary scene was a discipline" ([An Introduction to Disciplinarity](/post/introduction-to-disciplinarity#p-57)).

What sets off a new disciplinary space is a failure of attention. Normally we look at a center and pay no attention to the margins we are looking from. When the center stops holding our attention, "we now attend to what we were attending from. Whatever gesture from the margins redirects our attention in some shared way establishes a new center, and that's the disciplinary space: the scene of worship, or of inquiry, or love" ([Exodus from the Dead End of History](/post/exodus-from-the-dead-end-of-history#p-14)). The scientific laboratory is one version of this. So is a congregation, and so is a couple trying to work out whether they can trust each other.

Katz separates disciplinary spaces from the institutional disciplines (sociology, philosophy and the rest) that harden out of them. "A disciplinary space serves the center by inquiring into commands from the center," while a discipline tends to subordinate the center to its own object and set itself up as the judge of legitimacy ([Prolegomena](/post/prolegomena-to-the-study-of-the-origins-of-the-disciplines-gablog#p-5)). The work he proposes is to open new disciplinary spaces inside the established disciplines. That means taking their key terms, which mostly descend from the metalanguage of literacy, and turning them back on the discipline itself until they can issue workable imperatives again.

In practice, this means treating every utterance as belonging to some scene of inquiry. It also means asking what the center is commanding, and helping others to discover something they couldn't have seen on their own.

To read next, [An Introduction to Disciplinarity](/post/introduction-to-disciplinarity) is Katz's fullest treatment. It covers how disciplines turn into bureaucracies and how new disciplinary spaces resist that.

justice.q: What does Center Study mean by justice?
justice.a:
Katz treats justice less as a timeless ideal than as a historical solution to a problem the originary scene doesn't have. On the originary scene, and in ritual orders, distribution comes straight from the center: everyone who issues the sign gets a share. Once a human occupies the center and sacral kingship breaks down, the person at the center and the center as such no longer coincide. "Justice" is the first attempt to reconcile them. In Katz's words, "'Justice' is the subsistent center, to which the occupant of the center is subordinated" ([Distribution from the Center](/post/distribution-from-the-center#p-8)). The structure of distribution is unchanged, but what gets handed out is now different: "access to a mode of decision making, a recognition of something like a 'right'" (same paragraph). This is why justice divides people. Anyone can turn the concept to their own claim against the ruler, and that opens the way to *imperium in imperio*, a sovereignty within sovereignty.

The more constructive side lies in his account of the juridical. Courts sit between two thresholds. Below is the vendetta, private revenge between kin and groups. Above is the "antinomic" attack on the order itself, which ends in putting the king on trial. Justice holds the space between them. It is never exact: "justice is more of a rule of thumb than a precise science" ([The Tokenization of Resentment](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment#p-11)). It is also self-cancelling. If judgments became certain and expected, cases would stop arising, so "the perfection of the juridical would then be its abolition" ([If… Then](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack#p-4)).

This bears directly on resentment. A feeling of injustice is resentment toward the center for failing to uphold its own terms. Katz's advice is to "donate" any resentment the institutions can't absorb, rather than turning it into a call for revenge. He also argues that the "victimary" turns the juridical itself into a vehicle for vendetta ([Modeling Thirdness 2](/post/modeling-thirdness-2#p-2)).

Read [Distribution from the Center](/post/distribution-from-the-center) next. It is short and lays out the whole move from ritual sharing to rights.

center-study.q: What does Center Study mean by center study?
center-study.a:
"Center study" is Katz's name for his own development of the originary hypothesis, and the name says what it studies. Every human scene is organized around a center. On the originary scene this is the shared object whose appropriation everyone defers. Later it is the "occupied" center of chiefs, kings and states, and also every local center of attention. Center study follows the imperatives that come from that center as they pass through institutions. In Katz's words, it "traces the commands of the center, from the demarcations of the nomos through the histories of succession, to the treatment and preparation of disputes that look to be if they are not actually to be decided by the center" ([Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-substack#p-18)). In plain terms, the nomos is the founding distribution of land and authority, and succession is how the center passes from one occupant to the next.

Why a new name rather than "Generative Anthropology"? Katz marks the break explicitly. One impetus "for separating center studies from generative anthropology was the inadequate and impressionistic discussions of resentment in the latter," together with GA's trouble "scaling up," since it modeled everything on the small group of the originary scene ([The Tokenization of Resentment](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment#p-1)). Center study keeps the hypothesis but turns it toward power, law, money and technology. Katz also says he doesn't mind if people keep calling it GA.

It also understands itself in a particular way: as an idiom, not a master theory. Katz calls it "a kind of programming idiom to be made interoperable with other idioms. Less 'meta' than 'infra'" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-18)). It does not translate every other discourse into its own terms. Instead it enters them and asks what "would count as everyone saying the same thing so that everyone doesn't do the same thing at the same time." That phrase is his compressed version of what the originary sign accomplished.

To read next: [Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center), which builds the concept of the center from the ground up and shows why "all of our thoughts and deeds are of the center."

liberalism.q: What does Center Study mean by liberalism?
liberalism.a:
For Center Study, liberalism is not mainly a set of ideas about freedom and rights. It is a way that power works while denying it is power. Its basic categories (the individual, rights, equality, consent) imagine a person who exists before and outside any center. Katz argues there is no such person, because every human scene is organized around a center. So liberalism has to be described by what it does rather than by what it says. Katz's most compact definition is "liberalism, understood here as the process of centralization through equalization—intermediate layers of power and responsibility are continually hacked away so that central power can be exercised directly on all subjects" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-69)).

The paradox is that each new right, each new equalization, increases the reach of the state that has to enforce it. Families, guilds, churches, local authorities and other differentiated bodies get dissolved into equivalent units. In Katz's phrase, "Liberalism is essentially a process of pulverizing irreplaceables into interchangeables" ([Hostages, Proxies, and Moles](/post/hostages-proxies-and-moles#p-10)). Meanwhile the occupant of the center is made deliberately temporary and contestable, so resentment toward whoever holds power becomes the normal political condition.

That is why Katz calls liberalism parasitic rather than a stable order of its own: "liberalism is intrinsically parasitic: it needs a center to be de-centered" ([The Counter-Inquisition](/post/the-counter-inquisition-gablog#p-1)). It lives off centers it did not build and could not build. It also dissolves meaning, because its key words point at no shared ostensive, at no specific thing people can look at together. A "right" has stopped meaning a recognized customary claim and now names a new demand made against the existing order ([The Meaning of Meaning, and Metalanguage](/post/the-meaning-of-meaning-and-metalanguage#p-8)).

The alternative Katz proposes is not a return to some lost past. His position is to acknowledge the center that is always already there and to make power and responsibility explicit and matched to each other.

To read next, try [Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf), which follows how "rights talk" works in practice to build up central power.
